content: Drug susceptibility testing (DST) and the diagnosis of tuberculosis (TB) should be prioritized in all healthcare settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended several advanced methods for DST, which have been developed through recent technological advancements in laboratory diagnostics. These methods significantly reduce the time between TB detection and the diagnosis of drug resistance. Rapid DST methods enable timely selection of appropriate treatment regimens based on a patient’s drug resistance profile and can be feasibly implemented in diverse global settings. The expanded capacity for DST also enhances the ability to conduct drug resistance surveillance. WHO has endorsed new nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), such as the Xpert® MTB/RIF assay, which is a fully automated test that integrates sputum processing, DNA extraction, amplification, and detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance. This cartridge-based system detects common mutations in the rpoB gene in both smear-positive and smear-negative sputum samples, providing results in approximately 90 minutes. While Xpert MTB/RIF has significantly reduced the time required for accurate TB and rifampicin resistance diagnosis, additional DST methods may be necessary to assess resistance to other first-line and second-line drugs. Molecular line probe assays (LPAs) are another genotypic method for DST, endorsed by WHO for detecting M. tuberculosis and mutations conferring resistance to anti-TB drugs. LPAs are suitable for testing smear-positive sputum samples or M. tuberculosis cultures for rifampicin resistance alone or in combination with isoniazid resistance. However, LPAs are less sensitive for detecting isoniazid resistance, potentially underestimating resistance levels. These assays require technical expertise in molecular techniques and proper laboratory facilities. Phenotypic DST methods, including liquid and solid culture techniques, remain essential for determining drug resistance. Liquid culture methods are more sensitive and faster than solid culture methods, with pulmonary TB confirmation typically achieved within two weeks and DST results available in an additional one to two weeks. However, these methods are costly and require optimized specimen processing to minimize contamination. Solid culture methods, such as the proportion method, resistance ratio method, and absolute concentration method, are widely used due to their low cost and standardization. However, they require up to eight weeks for TB confirmation and an additional six weeks for DST results. The selection of drugs for susceptibility testing depends on the survey objectives and logistical considerations. For determining the burden of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), testing for rifampicin and isoniazid resistance is the minimum requirement. In settings with limited laboratory capacity, rifampicin susceptibility testing can serve as an initial screening, with further testing for isoniazid resistance in rifampicin-resistant strains. MDR-TB strains should also be tested for susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents, especially in the context of extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). Molecular-based DST methods, such as GeneXpert instruments, require verification tests upon installation and regular monitoring of performance indicators. For culture-based DST, the quality of culture media and drug dilutions must be controlled, and testing should include reference strains with known resistance profiles. Ethical considerations are paramount in drug resistance surveillance and surveys. Patient confidentiality must be respected, and informed consent should be obtained whenever feasible. Surveillance activities should aim to provide access to appropriate treatment for patients identified with drug-resistant TB. WHO recommends that all countries establish MDR-TB treatment programs or plans to implement them, using surveillance data to guide the development of diagnostic and treatment services. Conducting drug resistance surveys requires careful planning, including the formation of a national coordination team, defining survey objectives, and developing a diagnostic testing algorithm.
